title: What's the Caddy mechanism for ensuring that the Middleware instance created with parseCaddyfile will be used for ServeHTTP() rather than my Middleware instances created with New() returned in the ModuleInfo()?

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
The Caddyfile adapter handles the magic of you. See the code for the `RegisterHandlerDirective` here:

https://github.com/caddyserver/caddy/blob/master/caddyconfig%2Fhttpcaddyfile%2Fdirectives.go#L115-L137

It'll call your Caddyfile parser func, then calls `NewRoute`. The `NewRoute` method _does_ call the `New()` func, but see here:

https://github.com/caddyserver/caddy/blob/master/caddyconfig%2Fhttpcaddyfile%2Fdirectives.go#L274-L299

It only uses it to identify your module name, nothing more.

By the way, you can ask these questions in the Caddy forum at https://caddy.community 🙂

comments.body: The Caddyfile adapter runs as a separate step, all it does it produce a JSON config (all structs used to produce that config are thrown away), and then that JSON config gets loaded and run. You cannot expect the same struct to be used between adapting and running.

comments.body:
Did you use `json` struct tags on the config fields? Did you make them public/exported (uppercase first letter)? That's necessary so that it marshals to JSON properly. You can use `caddy adapt -p` to see how it looks when adapted to JSON. If it's missing anything, then it won't work.

You'll need to share more of your code for us to help probably.

comments.author: reporter
participant1
comments.body:
The object you build in `parseCaddyfile` is marshalled into its JSON representation in this line of `NewRoute`:

https://github.com/caddyserver/caddy/blob/9753c4451077d4459ec10cb3df27ab9dc4456290/caddyconfig/httpcaddyfile/directives.go#L295

Then Caddy unmarshalls the JSON into the object of your module, calls `Provision` on the object, and uses that object moving forward. That's why Francis said your configuration fields need to have at least their first letter uppercased and have `json` tags. I recommend you go through this blog post by the Go team: [JSON and Go](https://go.dev/blog/json).

comments.author: participant2
comments.body:
Without seeing the codebase as a whole, I'm having a really hard time following the logic here.

Your Caddy config structs _should_ have `json` struct tags. See https://caddyserver.com/docs/extending-caddy#configuration which shows that.

> It's a bit awkward to impose the requirement that the Caddyfile config fields should be exactly one-to-one mapping to my internal struct fields.

I don't understand what you mean by this. Why would that "requirement" exist? Your Caddy config struct is your Caddy config struct. There should be no such thing as a "Caddyfile config" struct, your Caddyfile parsing function would just parse the config arguments as text performing any necessary transformation (e.g. duration or byte size strings to plain integers, etc) and then the Caddyfile adapter will serialize it to JSON. But it can only serialize to JSON if you actually declared the `json` struct tags.

> why should I have to additionally ensure that the Caddyfile config should work well with the JSON adapter?

I don't understand that question. The entire point of the Caddyfile adapter is to produce a JSON config. Caddy does not run on Caddyfile, it runs on JSON config which is unmarshaled into Go structs.

comments.author: participant2
comments.body:
> what if the json/struct field points to another json object?

Then the child struct should also have JSON tags. The entire config structure of your module needs to be JSON serializable.

> https://caddyserver.com/docs/config-adapters says that the caddyfile is the standard adapter.

Standard means it ships with Caddy by default, as in not provided via a plugin.

You should not have `NewXAuth()` that you call in `parseCaddyfile`. It seems like you're doing that to set defaults. You shouldn't do that, your defaults should be set in your `Provision()` which is run at runtime when loading the config.

The Caddyfile parsing step's job is to take the tokens from the Caddyfile config and apply any that appear to a struct, and leave anything not specified by the user as the zero value (`""` for strings, 0 for numbers, false for booleans, etc). That way all defaults are handled only once in `Provision`, regardless of whether a Caddyfile or JSON or whatever other adapter was used.

> I am confused why this already instantiated XAuthMiddleware struct can not be reused further by Caddy instead of doing what you mentioned above:

Separation of concerns. Like we've repeated multiple times, the Caddyfile adapter's job is to produce a JSON config. That's it. Caddy actually runs on JSON config, because it allows for the admin API and makes it so the code can directly interact with Go structs with JSON tags. This is very normal, standard Go language stuff.

comments.author: participant2
comments.body:
That's wrong. That's not how you should manage config.

- Struct starts with zero values
- UnmarshalCaddyfile only overrides properties that appear in the Caddyfile
- Provision looks at any struct fields that should have defaults but that are still zero, and sets them to their defaults.

This approach is the most compatible way, with the least amount of code. It ensures both Caddyfile and JSON configs work and have defaults set properly, and ensures the Caddyfile-adapter-produced-JSON is as small as possible (only having properties that the user actually configured and nothing else).

This is how Caddy modules were designed to be written.

comments.author: participant2
comments.body:
> what is the rationale to create multiple instance of my plugin during its lifetime

Because the Caddyfile adapter may be performed in an entirely different process from the one the Caddy server actually runs in. If you use `caddy reload --config /etc/caddy/Caddyfile` then that runs a CLI process which adapts the Caddyfile (or returns errors if necessary) then makes an HTTP request to the _actually running_ Caddy process at its admin endpoint to push the JSON config to do a zero downtime reload.

Like I said before, separation of concerns. The Caddyfile adapter is entirely separate from runtime.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
To aid you with the design, your struct should have fields for the user configuration, and those are exported with JSON tags (the JSON tags allow for friendly JSON field naming and other options). These act as the configuration message channel between you and the users. It's also helpful to [make the zero values useful](https://<redacted-host>/watch?v=PAAkCSZUG1c&t=385s). nil pointer, empty string, 0, and false can be signals of users wanting the default values. The Caddyfile unmarshaller should act only as an adapter from the more user-friendly format of Caddyfile to the programmatic config format of JSON, because JSON is the native configuration language of Caddy.

In Provision, you're expected to pick up the public/exported fields of the struct (remember, those are user entry points), check whatever default values to be assumed, and translate the public fields to unexported fields (if necessary) that are necessary for the actual operation of the module. For example, the user doesn't need to know of a mutex' presence in the struct, but you might need to initialize one in `Provision` because locking is necessary part of the module operation. So, you have configuration vs. function.

As for the 3rd-party struct, you don't have to expose it directly, but you can (and recommended) abstract it with your own fields in your struct, and then that 3rd-party struct will have an **un**exported instance in your struct that you will fill based on the user's input in your struct.

There's a lot of separation of concern involved. Configuration -> Adapt (if necessary) -> Provision (prepare internal state for operation) -> Validation (e.g. check DB is reachable)  -> Operation (uses internal state set in provision).

comments.body:
Something like this:

```go
type XAuthMiddleware struct {
	SessionConfig *SessionConfig `json:"session,omitempty"`
	OidcConfig    *OIDCConfig    `json:"oidc,omitempty"`
	TokenConfig   *TokenConfig   `json:"token,omitempty"`

	logger         *zap.Logger
	sessionManager *MySessionManager
}

type SessionConfig struct {
	CookieName        string         `json:"cookie_name,omitempty"`
	Secure            bool           `json:"secure,omitempty"`
	HTTPOnly          bool           `json:"http_only,omitempty"`
	SameSite          string         `json:"same_site,omitempty"` // could be an enum, I dunno
	MaxTimeout        caddy.Duration `json:"max_timeout,omitempty"`
	InactivityTimeout caddy.Duration `json:"inactivity_timeout,omitempty"`
	IPCheck           bool           `json:"ip_check,omitempty"`
}

type TokenConfig struct {
	SignKey   string `json:"sign_key,omitempty"`
	SignAlg   string `json:"sign_alg,omitempty"`
	JWTHeader string `json:"jwt_header,omitempty"`
	UID       string `json:"uid,omitempty"`
	Roles     string `json:"roles,omitempty"`
}

type OIDCConfig struct {
	ClientID      string   `json:"client_id,omitempty"`
	ClientSecret  string   `json:"client_secret,omitempty"`
	RedirectURI   string   `json:"redirect_uri,omitempty"`
	AuthEndpoint  string   `json:"auth_endpoint,omitempty"`
	TokenEndpoint string   `json:"token_endpoint,omitempty"`
	Scopes        []string `json:"scopes,omitempty"`
}

type MySessionManager struct {
	*scs.SessionManager //external dependency on  https://github.com/alexedwards/scs/blob/master/session.go#L16
}
```

Notice that the config structs are _just config_, and the `MySessionManager` should only be initialized during `Provision()` and be fed any config options from `SessionConfig` as necessary.

Also you should use `caddy.Duration` type for any times, which is a super-type of `time.Duration` (Go stdlib) so then you can parse Caddyfile config like `inactivity_timeout 30s` which automatically multiplies `30` by `seconds`, you could also do `1h` (hour) etc or `500ms`, etc.

Look through Caddy's source to find examples. There's tons.

comments.author: participant2
comments.body:
To clarify, Caddy's native config language is JSON. That's what Caddy actually runs on. The Caddyfile is there as a UX layer to make it easier for 99% of users to use Caddy and write more natural-reading configs. 

Yes, some users prefer to write JSON config directly, especially if they plan on using Caddy's admin API to perform dynamic/scripted config changes programmatically.

The `caddy adapt` command only runs the Caddyfile adapter and emits the output JSON to stdout. That's it. It's useful to test that your UnmarshalCaddyfile is working correctly (you can have assertions that a given Caddyfile matches an expected JSON output).

The `caddy reload` command only works if you already have Caddy running (i.e. with `caddy run`), it adapts then pushes the JSON config to the running Caddy server over the admin API (the /load endpoint, see https://caddyserver.com/docs/api) which performs a zero downtime in-memory config swap where for a moment two config copies are running at once during the handover. https://caddyserver.com/docs/architecture explains how that works. 

You shouldn't name your JSON config "caddyfile.json" because it's not a Caddyfile, it's a JSON config. That filename is ambiguous.
